questions.prompt: For a fixed multiplier, the dual function is
questions.explanation: The dual function holds the multipliers fixed and minimizes the Lagrangian in the decision variable. A feasible primal value is an upper number on the optimal value, not this construction. The supremum would reverse the problem and need not be a lower bound. Equality with the primal optimal value is strong duality, which needs extra conditions. The dual function itself is only the infimum.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
options: the primal objective evaluated only at feasible points
the supremum of the Lagrangian over the decision variable
the infimum of the Lagrangian over the decision variable
always equal to the primal optimal value

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x^2\) subject to \(x \ge 3\). The Lagrangian is \(x^2 + u(3 - x)\) with \(u \ge 0\). What lower bound does \(u = 2\) give?
questions.explanation: Stationarity in \(x\) is \(2x - u = 0\), so \(x = u/2\). Substituting produces the dual function \(3u - u^2/4\). At \(u = 2\) that value is \(6 - 1 = 5\). The primal optimum is \(9\), at \(x = 3\), so \(5\) sits strictly below it, which is what a non-optimal multiplier does. Reporting \(9\) gives the primal value. Reporting \(4\) is \(u^2\). Reporting \(2\) is the multiplier itself.

questions.prompt: Weak duality says that every dual-feasible multiplier gives
questions.explanation: The Lagrangian at a primal-feasible point is at most the objective when inequality multipliers are nonnegative, because each inequality term is nonpositive. Minimizing the Lagrangian can only make the number smaller, so the dual function sits at or below the primal optimal value. It is not an upper bound. The \(x\) that attains the infimum need not satisfy the constraints. Equality multipliers are free. Their sign is not part of dual feasibility.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that builds the dual of a minimization with inequalities \(g(x) \le 0\). Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The Lagrangian has to exist before it can be minimized in \(x\). That minimization, with the multiplier held fixed, is the dual function, so the sign restriction comes after the function has been formed. Only then does the dual problem maximize it. Maximizing before the infimum would still be a joint problem in \(x\), not the dual. Restricting the sign before the Lagrangian is written does not yet produce a function of \(u\).

steps: Attach a multiplier \(u\) to \(g\) and form the Lagrangian \(f(x) + u\, g(x)\).
With that Lagrangian in hand, minimize it in \(x\) while holding \(u\) fixed.
Keep only the multipliers \(u \ge 0\), the ones dual feasibility allows for this inequality.
Maximize the resulting dual function over those remaining multipliers.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x^2\) subject to \(x \ge 3\). The primal optimal value is \(9\), and the dual function is \(3u - u^2/4\). Which statements are true?
questions.explanation:
Substitute the stated multipliers into \(3u - u^2/4\).
• \(u = 4\) gives \(12 - 4 = 8\).
• \(u = 6\) gives \(18 - 9 = 9\), matching the primal value.
• Weak duality puts every value at a nonnegative multiplier at or below \(9\).
• \(u = 2\) gives \(5\), not \(9\).
• A negative multiplier is not dual feasible for a \(\le\) constraint written in the Lagrangian as \(u(3-x)\).
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
options: At \(u = 4\) the dual function equals \(8\).
At \(u = 2\) the dual function equals \(9\).
\(u = -2\) is dual feasible.
At \(u = 6\) the dual function equals the primal optimal value.
Every dual-feasible value is at most \(9\).

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x^2\) subject to \(x \ge a\), with \(a > 0\). Using the multiplier \(u \ge 0\) on \(a - x\), the dual function equals
questions.explanation: The Lagrangian is \(x^2 + u(a - x)\). Its derivative in \(x\) is \(2x - u\), so the infimum occurs at \(x = u/2\). Substituting leaves \(a u - u^2/4\). On the declared ranges this value is finite and positive. Replacing the minus by a plus double-counts the square. Dropping \(a\) leaves only the quadratic term, which is not the infimum. Evaluating the Lagrangian at \(x = a\) instead of at \(x = u/2\) computes a feasible primal number, not the dual function.

questions.prompt: A note derives the dual of minimizing \(x^2\) subject to \(x \ge 3\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The Lagrangian and the stationarity equation match \(x^2 + u(3-x)\). Dual feasibility keeps \(u\) nonnegative because the constraint was written as \(3-x \le 0\). The false step is the substitution. \((u/2)^2 + u(3 - u/2) = u^2/4 + 3u - u^2/2 = 3u - u^2/4\). The squared term is subtracted, not added.

steps: Stationarity in \(x\) gives \(2x - u = 0\), so \(x = u/2\).
Substituting that \(x\) produces the dual function \(3u + u^2/4\).
Dual feasibility for this inequality requires \(u \ge 0\).
reasons: The substitution equals \(3u - u^2/4\). The squared term is subtracted.
Dual feasibility allows a negative multiplier here.

questions.prompt: The same problem has primal optimal value \(9\). The multiplier \(u = 4\) produces dual value \(8\). What is the duality gap?
questions.explanation: The gap is the primal optimal value minus the dual value, \(9 - 8 = 1\). Both numbers are given by the problem, and weak duality says the difference cannot be negative. Reporting \(8\) or \(9\) repeats one of the two values. Reporting \(17\) adds them. The gap is zero only at a multiplier that attains \(9\), and \(u = 4\) is not that multiplier.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The dual problem, once the dual function is known, is
questions.explanation: Building the dual function already minimized out the decision variable. What remains is a maximization over the multipliers that keep the infimum finite and satisfy the sign restrictions. Minimizing the dual function would run away from the primal value. A joint minimization is the Lagrangian problem before the infimum is taken. Maximizing the primal objective is a different problem, and for a minimization primal it is not the dual.

questions.prompt: An inequality \(g(x) \le 0\) and an equality \(h(x) = 0\) differ, in the dual, by
questions.explanation: Nonnegativity is what makes the inequality term \(u\, g(x)\) nonpositive at a feasible point, and that is the source of the lower bound. An equality is zero on the feasible set for either sign of its multiplier, so that multiplier stays free. Forcing it to zero deletes the constraint. Dropping the inequality from the Lagrangian deletes the lower-bound term. Requiring both multipliers to be negative reverses the inequality.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(x^2\) subject to \(x \ge 5\). Using the Lagrangian \(x^2 + u(5 - x)\), what lower bound does \(u = 4\) give?
questions.explanation: The same completion gives the dual function \(5u - u^2/4\). At \(u = 4\) the value is \(20 - 4 = 16\). The unconstrained minimizer of the Lagrangian is \(x = 2\), which is not primal feasible, and that is allowed: the dual function minimizes over every \(x\). The feasible value \(x = 5\) gives the primal number \(25\), which is not this lower bound. Reporting \(4\) gives the multiplier. Reporting \(20\) stops before subtracting the square.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: Applying the same Lagrangian construction to a linear program produces
questions.explanation: The Lagrangian of a linear objective with linear constraints is linear in the decision variable. Minimizing it in that variable is finite only on a set of linear inequalities in the multipliers, and the resulting dual function is linear. The dual is therefore a linear program. It is not a nonconvex quadratic. The auxiliary start-up problem and a single reduced-cost vector are simplex constructions. They are not the dual program obtained from the Lagrangian.
